messages:
alex_r: heads up — ran an nsys capture trying to repro the KV-cache warmup hotspot. weird sampling bias, short sample windows seem to miss the kernel handoff. anyone seen this before?

kevin: yep, seen that. short windows + immediate tracing often snap the warmup out of the picture. what flags did you use?

alex_r: started with this quick command:
```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --duration=10s --output=kv-warmup.qdrep ./run_inference.sh
```
just wanted a quick smoke capture.

samira: two immediate problems: 1) 10s is usually too short for batched workloads that have passive warmup, 2) OSRT sampling + short duration biases toward steady-state kernels and skips the early kernel-selection transitions.

kevin: try bracketed capture: warmup for ~30s without tracing then capture a 20–40s window. e.g.:
```
# warm up first (no nsys)
./run_inference.sh --warmup-reqs 200
# then capture
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --duration=30s --output=kv-bracket.qdrep ./run_inference.sh --replay 100
```
that usually surfaces the kernel handoff.

alex_r: good point. i also noticed that when batching ramps up we get repeated small kernels with identical names but different launch shapes — makes the timeline noisy. any quick tips to aggregate those in UI or CLI?

samira: in the UI you can group by kernel name and then sort by accumulated time. CLI approach: export a timeline CSV and post-process by (kernel-name, grid, block) signature to combine runs. rough example:
```
nsys stats -r gpukernsum kv-bracket.qdrep > kernel_summary.txt
# then awk/python to collapse by truncated kernel name + params
```

kevin: also check NVTX markers around batching boundaries and KV cache ops. if your runtime emits nvtx push/pop for batch start/end and kvcache insert/evict you can filter the capture to those regions with --capture-range or manually slice the qdrep in UI. helps isolate the handoff.

alex_r: i haven't been using NVTX for the cache ops — that's on me. is there a recommended NVTX tagging convention for batching/kvcache?

samira: we use short markers:
- NVTX "BATCH_START" / "BATCH_END" with metadata: batch_size
- NVTX "KV_INSERT" / "KV_EVICT" w/ keys hashed into attributes (no raw keys)
- NVTX "KERNEL_SELECT" w/ chosen kernel variant name

kevin: tag the warmup iterations too: NVTX "WARMUP_ITER" so you can filter traces and compare pre/post warmup kernel timelines.

alex_r: ok adding those. last question — sampling interval. some captures i've seen use a sampling rate flag (sample-interval=1000us?) what do we actually want for kernel hotspot detection without exploding file size?

samira: aim for a middle ground: 500–2000us sample interval is fine for our kernels; shorter if you're hunting microsecond spikes but qdrep size grows. couple rules:
- Longer duration + coarser sampling wins if you're after overall kernel selection patterns.
- Short interval + bracketed window wins if looking for short-lived kernel spikes.

kevin: can also use selective tracing: trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt but drop globs for noisy GPU driver telemetry if it's not helpful. and don't forget to disable verbose host-side sampling unless you need CPU stacks.

perf-bot: automated note — kv-bracket.qdrep captured (size 1.2GB), GPU time dominated by small kernel "k_pack_v1" (34%), followed by "k_shmem_shuffle" (18%). NVTX markers present: BATCH_START/BATCH_END.

alex_r: perf-bot output helps. i see k_pack_v1 dominating early in the capture but later a different kernel "k_pack_v2_q4" takes over. sounds like kernel selection switch tied to batch size or kv hit-rate.

samira: exactly. kernel selection heuristic in the runtime checks kv-cache hits and sequence length distribution; if your cache warms up it flips to a lower-latency kernel. that flip can be invisible with short traces.

kevin: follow-up experiment idea: force two runs with identical input stream but pre-populate KV cache in one run and leave cold in another. capture both with same bracketed window and compare timelines. that'll show the selection delta cleanly.

alex_r: nice. i'll do: prepopulate by replaying 500 warmup queries, capture the next 30s; then cold run capture without warmup. will post results. thanks for the pointers. :rocket:

samira: one last tip — when you suspect kernel selection regression after a change, run differential capture on the same machine (pin CPU/GPU freq) and include environment snapshot (driver, CUDA, ML kernels). small env differences can change kernel fallback.

kevin: and file the qdrep + a short reproduction script in the perf regression issue so reviewers can open in Nsight with the same view.

alex_r: will do. posting backlog link once uploads finish.

perf-bot: reminder — large qdrep files are auto-archived after 7d in perf-bucket. if you want retained longer tag with @infra-retain.
